title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT): Ophthalmic Implications & Perioperative Care
summary: While often viewed as a systemic condition, Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is a critical concern for the ophthalmic surgeon regarding perioperative risk, anticoagulation management, and the shared pathophysiology with Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO). This guide bridges the gap between systemic thromboembolism and ophthalmic practice.

sections.title: Definition & Ophthalmic Relevance
sections.content: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within the deep venous system, most commonly in the lower extremities. In ophthalmology, it is relevant for: 1) Perioperative management of patients on systemic anticoagulants; 2) Post-operative risk in prolonged orbital or reconstructive surgeries; and 3) Shared hypercoagulable risk factors with Retinal Vein Occlusions (RVO).

branches: Stasis of Blood Flow (Immobility, Obstructive tumors, Post-op bed rest)
Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S deficiency, Malignancy, Pregnancy)

sections.title: The Ocular Link: DVT and Retinal Vein Occlusion
content: Patients with DVT/PE have a higher Hazard Ratio (approx 1.5) for developing RVO.
Shared Risk Factors: Hypertension, Diabetes, Hyperlipidemia.
Thrombophilia screen (Factor V Leiden, Antiphospholipid Ab) indicated in young patients (<50) with RVO.
The presence of RVO should prompt a review of the patient's systemic VTE history.

sections.title: Wells Clinical Prediction Rule for DVT

rows: Paralysis, Paresis, or Immobilization of lower limb
Bedridden >3 days or Major Surgery within 12 weeks
Localized tenderness along the deep venous system
Calf swelling >3cm compared to asymptomatic side
Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg
Alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT

sections.title: Clinical Features of DVT
content: Unilateral leg pain and tenderness.
Swelling (Edema) of the calf or thigh.
Warmth and erythema over the affected area.
Homan's Sign: Pain in calf upon dorsiflexion of the foot (Low sensitivity).
Distended superficial veins.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment (Wells Score calculation)
Step 2: D-Dimer Assay (High sensitivity, low specificity; used to rule out in low-risk pts)
Step 3: Compression Ultrasonography (CUS) - Gold standard bedside test
Step 4: CT Venography or MRI (Used if CUS is inconclusive or for pelvic DVT)
Step 5: Venography (Historical gold standard, now rarely used)

sections.title: RED FLAG: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
content: Sudden onset Dyspnea (Shortness of breath)
Pleuritic Chest Pain
Hemoptysis (Coughing up blood)
Tachycardia & Tachypnea
Syncope or Sudden Death

Stop anticoagulants; bridge therapy usually required

sections.title: Medication Guide: Systemic Anticoagulation
content: Unfractionated Heparin: Rapid onset, reversible with Protamine.
Enoxaparin (LMWH): 1mg/kg BID (Treatment) or 40mg QD (Prophylaxis).
Warfarin: Vitamin K antagonist; monitor INR (Goal 2.0-3.0).
DOACs (Apixaban/Rivaroxaban): No monitoring required; specific reversal agents (Andexanet alfa) now available.

sections.title: Bridge Therapy Protocol
content: 1. Stop Warfarin 5 days before high-risk ophthalmic surgery.
2. Start therapeutic LMWH 3 days before surgery.
3. Last dose of LMWH 24 hours prior to surgery.
4. Check INR on morning of surgery (Target <1.5).
5. Resume LMWH and Warfarin 12-24 hours post-operatively once hemostasis is secured.

sections.title: Key Ophthalmic Clinical Pearls
content: Regional anesthesia (Peribulbar/Retrobulbar) in anticoagulated patients carries a higher risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage.
Sub-Tenon's or Topical anesthesia is preferred for patients with DVT on blood thinners.
In Orbital Compartment Syndrome (OCS) secondary to hemorrhage, emergent lateral canthotomy/cantholysis is mandatory regardless of DVT history.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Studies
content: BRIDGE Trial: Showed that for many patients with AFib, bridging with LMWH increased bleeding without reducing VTE—leads to more conservative bridging in eye surgery.
COMPASS Trial: Low-dose Rivaroxaban + Aspirin reduces major adverse limb and cardiovascular events but increases bleeding risk.
ORBIT Study: Investigated VTE risk in oculoplastic surgery; highlighted importance of early mobilization.

sections.title: Emergency Signs: Orbital Hemorrhage
content: Sudden Proptosis and Deep Pain
Rock-hard globe on palpation
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD)
Vision Loss/Decreased Color Vision
Nausea/Vomiting (Oculocardiac reflex)

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
sections.content: Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS) occurs in 20-50% of DVT patients, causing chronic leg pain and ulcers. In ophthalmic terms, if DVT is secondary to a hypercoagulable state, the risk of bilateral RVO or CRAO is significantly elevated. Recurrence of VTE is 10% in the first year without anticoagulation.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: DVT is rare in children but increasing in tertiary care settings. In pediatric RVO (rare), a full DVT/VTE workup is mandatory. Causes often involve central venous catheters, nephrotic syndrome, or inherited thrombophilias like Factor V Leiden or G20210A prothrombin mutation.
